people.name: Surjit S. Bhalla
people.role: Economist and columnist. He chairs the Technical Expert Group for the first official Household Income Survey of India, and was a part-time member of the Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister until December 2018.
people.intro: The quotations are from his Indian Express column of 17 October 2026, the longer version he published on Substack the same day, and his Indian Express column of 24 October, a reply to Jean Drèze and Yogendra Yadav. He sets each state's final roll against a clean roll, his estimate of what a roll should hold once adults who do not register are allowed for. He put the eligible people kept off the rolls in nine states at about 70 lakh on 17 October and at about 1 crore on 24 October. He also criticises how the revision was run.

pieces.title: An entitled generation and an Opposition that protests too much
Much Ado About (Almost) Nothing
SIR needs reform. But let’s go by numbers, not protestors’ slogans

claims.quote: In India, registration is voluntary; you fill in Form 6 if you want to vote. The ECI’s own pre-SIR data showed that in the 2024 Lok Sabha election, one in four Indians aged 18 to 29, 73 million young people, were not registered. Add a small allowance for older adults who have never registered, or who dropped off after moving, and about 8.5 per cent of adults are legitimately not on the rolls.
claims.rests: It rests on the Commission's count of electors aged 18 to 29 on the 2024 roll, set against his own estimate of young adults, and an allowance of 1 per cent of adults for older people off the roll, which is his judgement.
claims.site: No roll or population by age is at hand, so his 73 million cannot be checked. The totals set bounds on it. On the UN's estimate the national roll of 2024 held 96.3 names per 100 adults, a gap of 3.7 per 100. For 8.5 per 100 adults to have been off that roll, about 4.8 names per 100 adults on it would have to be people who had died, moved or been entered twice. Before the revision the rolls of the nine states he studies held 97.5 per cent of projected adults. Tamil Nadu (106.5 per cent) and Kerala (100.4 per cent) held more names than projected adults, which supports his view that some rolls carried names that should not have been there. The law gives both sides of his first sentence. A person who is not on the roll may apply under section 23 of the 1950 Act, and in an intensive revision the Rules have the roll prepared afresh, which is why the revision sent a form to every elector on the old roll.
claims.stops: The figures cannot show whether the young adults off the 2024 roll chose not to register or were never reached.

claims.quote: A clean roll for these states, built from each state’s adults less each state’s own non-registration, should hold about 535 million names; the final rolls hold 528 million. Allowing for the legitimate removal of non-citizens, the best estimate is that about 7 million eligible voters (range 1 to 13 million) have been excluded from the rolls without adequate explanation.
claims.rests: It rests on each state's projected adults less that state's own unregistered young adults and 1 per cent of adults, set against the final rolls, with states above his clean roll netted against states below it.
claims.site: His 528 million is the nine official final rolls with West Bengal counted at 6.77 crore. The Chief Electoral Officer's final roll for West Bengal holds 6,44,52,609 names, and adding the 32,68,119 found eligible after adjudication gives 6,77,20,728. His clean roll starts from his own count of adults in these states, 59.04 crore, scaled to his national total of 100.8 crore. The Technical Group's projection used on the All India page gives 60,12,56,000, about 1.1 crore more. On the official figures the nine final rolls hold 52,45,53,415 names, 12.8 per cent short of projected adults. With his national 8.5 per cent applied to every state, the final rolls are about 1.25 crore short after netting on his own count of adults, and about 2.6 crore short on the projected adults with the Chief Electoral Officer's final roll for West Bengal.
claims.stops: No registration by age and no count of people who are not citizens is at hand, so his clean roll for each state cannot be rebuilt. Whether Bihar's surplus names are migrant workers registered at home, as he says, the rolls cannot show.

claims.quote: The 130 million in the headlines counts every draft removal, in all three phases, before appeals. It is nearly twenty times the number of eligible voters removed.
claims.rests: It rests on the Commission's draft-stage total of 13.37 crore names, as Deccan Herald reported it, against his own 70 lakh.
claims.site: The states' own figures count 13,39,03,307 names left off the drafts in 31 states. Of them 2,79,69,558 were entered as dead and 1,01,48,459 as enrolled more than once. His ratio follows from his own two numbers, which cover different ground. The 70 lakh is for nine states with final rolls, after netting. The 13.39 crore covers 31 states before claims were heard, and nine of them had no final roll on 24 October 2026.
claims.stops: Neither count says how many of the people left off were entitled to stay on the roll.

claims.quote: But with only 60% of its young registered, a clean UP roll is about 85% of adults, and the final roll is within about 1.4 million of it.
claims.rests: His figure that only 60 per cent of Uttar Pradesh's adults aged 18 to 29 were on the 2024 roll comes from the Commission's Atlas, which is not at hand.
claims.site: Uttar Pradesh's final roll of 10 April 2026 holds 13,39,84,792 names against 16,16,85,000 projected adults, 82.9 per cent. His own count of Uttar Pradesh's adults is 15.9 crore, and his clean roll at 85 per cent of it is 13.53 crore, about 14 lakh above the final roll as he says. The same 85 per cent of the projection used on the All India page would be about 34 lakh above it. At his national 8.5 per cent of projected adults the clean roll would be 14.79 crore and the final roll 1.40 crore short of it. Before the revision Uttar Pradesh's roll held 95.5 per cent of projected adults. For only 60 per cent of the young to have been enrolled, between 1.7 and 1.9 crore of the older names on that roll, on the two counts of adults, would have to be people who had died, moved or been entered twice. At the draft the officers entered 46,23,796 as dead and 25,47,207 as enrolled more than once.
claims.stops: No figure says how many young adults in Uttar Pradesh chose not to register.

claims.quote: Of the 58 million names removed in these states, 51 million had to go: The dead, the duplicates, those who had moved away for good. Seven of every eight removals were justified.
claims.rests: It rests on the gap between the rolls before the revision and his clean roll.
claims.site: The nine rolls held 58,60,69,594 names before the revision. His 51 million is that total less his clean roll of 53.5 crore, so it is set by his benchmark. It does not count reasons. At the draft the officers gave reasons for the 7,19,68,121 names left off in these states. They entered 1,67,88,487 as dead and 51,02,375 as enrolled more than once, 2.19 crore together, and 5.01 crore as shifted, absent or other. For 51 million to be names that had to go, about 2.9 crore of the shifted, absent or other entries would have to be people who had moved for good.
claims.stops: The reason beside each name is what the officer wrote down, and nobody checked it.

claims.quote: In 2004, after the last nationwide intensive revision, the roll held 4.4 per cent more names than there were adults, 28 million phantom voters. It was 3.1 per cent too high in 2014.
claims.rests: It rests on the rolls of 2004 and 2014 set against his own estimate of adults, the census carried forward and corrected for its past overshoot.
claims.site: The same rolls set against the UN's estimate of adults give the opposite sign. The 2004 roll held 98.9 names per 100 adults and the 2014 roll 98.2. On the UN's figures the roll last held more names than adults in 1999, at 103.4. The roll counts are the same, so the difference lies in the estimate of adults, which is also what his 70 lakh rests on. His own table puts India's adults in 2024 at 97.9 crore, against the UN's 101.8 crore, so on his count the 2024 roll held about as many names as there were adults.
claims.stops: Each comparison holds only if its population estimate is right, and the two estimates differ by a few per cent.

claims.quote: in West Bengal, 6 to 7 per cent of adults (about 5 million eligible citizens) appear to have been removed without adequate explanation
claims.rests: It rests on a clean West Bengal roll of 7.33 crore, built from the high registration of its young adults in 2024, against a final roll of 6.77 crore, less about 5 lakh people who are not citizens.
claims.site: The Chief Electoral Officer's final roll of 28 February 2026 held 6,44,52,609 names, with 60,06,675 held back for adjudication. Of those, 32,68,119 were found eligible and 27,16,393 not eligible, as reported. His 6.77 crore is the final roll plus those found eligible. The roll the 2026 election was held on held 6,82,51,008 names. Against 7,70,30,000 projected adults that roll is 11.4 per cent short, and the final roll 16.3 per cent. His clean roll less the election roll gives about 50 lakh, close to his figure.
claims.stops: No count of people who are not citizens and no split of West Bengal's deletions by religion has been found.

claims.quote: the process was hasty, demanded paperwork the poor and the migrant do not keep, and added a new declaration to Form 6 without a change in the rules, a move whose legality the Supreme Court has yet to decide.
But criticising the administration of an exercise is very different from claiming that it disenfranchised a seventh of the electorate. The evidence says the ECI has been much more right than wrong.
Put that column back, and DY's own numbers give the answer: About 1 crore disenfranchised, not 7.1 crore. The expected roll is 53.8 crore; the final roll is 52.8 crore.
claims.rests: It rests on his allowance for adults who would not be on any roll, 5.2 crore young adults off the 2024 rolls of these states and 1.5 per cent of adults for older people, taken from 59.9 crore projected adults. He gives the 59.9 crore as Drèze and Yadav's figure, and their table prints 60.12 crore.
claims.site: On his own adults the allowance comes to 6.1 crore and the expected roll to 53.8 crore, as he says. The projection of adults for the nine states used on the All India page is 60,12,56,000, the same figure as Drèze and Yadav's table, and with the same allowance it gives an expected roll of 54.0 crore. The official final rolls for the nine states total 52,45,53,415, with West Bengal at the Chief Electoral Officer's 6,44,52,609, and his 52.8 crore matches that total with West Bengal counted after adjudication. On the official figures the shortfall is about 1.57 crore, or 1.24 crore with West Bengal counted after adjudication. His column of 17 October put it at about 70 lakh, on 59.04 crore adults and an allowance of 1 per cent for older people.
claims.stops: No registration by age is at hand, so the 5.2 crore young adults off the roll cannot be checked, and a choice not to register cannot be told from an omission.

claims.quote: West Bengal, where the young register well, expected 7.4 crore and got 6.8: About 60 lakh short. And there the appeals failed: Of the 34 lakh Bengalis who appealed, The Economist reports, fewer than 0.05 per cent had their cases heard before election day, and the tribunals have since found 90 per cent of appellants valid all along.
claims.rests: It rests on his expected West Bengal roll of 7.4 crore and The Economist's figures for the appeals.
claims.site: West Bengal's final roll of 28 February 2026 held 6,44,52,609 names and the roll the election was held on 6,82,51,008, against 7,70,30,000 projected adults. His 7.4 crore less the election roll is 57.5 lakh, close to his 60 lakh. The official figures count 38,31,429 appeals, 22,21,118 of them by people who were excluded and 16,10,311 against inclusion. 1,607 people were restored before the poll, 0.04 per cent of all appeals and 0.07 per cent of those by the excluded. His 34 lakh matches neither count.
claims.stops: No outcome of tribunal decisions after the poll has been found, so the claim that 90 per cent of appellants were found valid cannot be checked.

claims.quote: Before the SIR, these nine states had 58.6 crore names on their rolls. A clean roll, the table shows, would hold 53.8 crore. The difference, nearly 5 crore names, was the dead, the departed and the duplicated, and this on rolls that still missed 5.2 crore young people.
claims.rests: It rests on the rolls before the revision against his clean roll of 53.8 crore.
claims.site: The nine rolls before the revision held 58,60,69,594 names, his 58.6 crore, which is 4.81 crore above his clean roll. At the draft the officers entered 1,67,88,487 people as dead and 51,02,375 as enrolled more than once in these states, 2.19 crore in all. The other 2.6 crore of his gap would have to come from people entered as shifted, absent or other.
claims.stops: No record says how many of the people entered as shifted or absent had in fact moved.

strongest: He keeps the draft-stage count of names left off apart from a count of eligible people kept off the rolls, as the figures here do.

His final rolls for eight of the nine states match the official figures, his 586 million before the revision is the official 58.61 crore, and his West Bengal appeals figures match the Commission's affidavit as reported.
Some rolls held more names than projected adults before the revision, Tamil Nadu at 106.5 per cent and Kerala at 100.4, so part of any fall there was names that should not have been on the roll.

He says the revision was hasty, asked the poor and migrants for papers they do not keep and added a declaration to Form 6 without a change in the Rules, and he asks the Commission to publish deletions by reason, state and booth.
On 24 October he puts the eligible voters wrongly left off the nine rolls at about 1 crore and says that inflating the number lets the Commission dismiss the real ones.
further: His 70 lakh rests on three choices. His own count of adults in the nine states is about 1.1 crore below the Technical Group's projection, his allowance for young adults off the roll is set state by state, and states with surplus names are netted against states that fall short. With his own 8.5 per cent applied to each state, the nine final rolls are about 1.25 crore short on his count of adults and about 2.6 crore short on the projection used on the All India page.

The 51 million that had to go is the gap between the old rolls and his clean roll. The officers entered 2.19 crore as dead or enrolled more than once, and the rest would have to come from entries of shifted, absent or other that nobody checked.
He treats young adults off the 2024 roll as people who chose not to register. In an intensive revision the Rules have the roll prepared afresh, and the figures cannot tell a choice from an omission.
His excess rolls in 2004 and 2014 come from his own estimate of adults. On the UN's estimate both rolls held fewer names than adults.
His West Bengal roll of 6.77 crore adds back the 32.7 lakh found eligible after the final roll was published.

His figure moved from about 70 lakh on 17 October to about 1 crore on 24 October when he raised his count of adults from 59.04 to 59.9 crore, raised his allowance for older people from 1 to 1.5 per cent and changed his count of young adults off the roll. On the projected count of adults the same method gives about 1.2 to 1.6 crore.

people.name: Jean Drèze
people.role: Jean Drèze is a visiting professor in the Department of Economics at Ranchi University.
people.intro: The quotations are from his column in The Economic Times of 21 October 2026, a follow-up to the column he wrote with Yogendra Yadav in The Indian Express. He sets the rolls of the major states against their projected adults before the revision and in the draft, and for the twelve states with final lists in the final lists too, and asks why the drafts fell so far below the adults.

pieces.title: Long & short of SIR: What happens when exclusion is prioritised over inclusion

claims.quote: In a recent article in The Indian Express, Yogendra Yadav and I defended the view that the SIR process is leading to mass disenfranchisement - at least 12 cr eligible voters (12% of India's estimated adult population) are likely to be left out of the final SIR lists.
claims.rests: It rests on the joint column's shortfall of almost 12 per cent in nine states, carried to the whole country.
claims.site: No national count of adults off the final rolls exists, because several states have no final roll yet. In the twelve states with final rolls and projected adults, the final rolls hold 87.5 per cent of projected adults, 8.36 crore short.
claims.stops: A projection counts residents, so the gap between it and a roll mixes adults wrongly left off, adults who were never enrolled and migrants enrolled in another state.

claims.quote: For all major states together, pre-SIR lists add up to 99% of the corresponding adult population (see table).
claims.rests: It rests on his table, the rolls before the revision against the Technical Group's projected adults for 2026, with Assam and Himachal Pradesh left out.
claims.site: Across the 19 states with projected adults, the rolls before the revision held 93,92,60,959 names against 95,50,92,000 adults, 98.3 per cent. Six of them held more names than projected adults, Telangana 115.2 per cent, Karnataka 106.8, Tamil Nadu 106.5, Odisha 101.7, Andhra Pradesh 100.7 and Kerala 100.4.
claims.stops: A projection counts residents, so a migrant counts where they live and the roll counts them where they are enrolled.

claims.quote: 13 cr is the official number of names on 'ASDD lists' - ASDD being 'absentee, shifted, duplicate or deceased' in EC lingo.
claims.rests: It rests on the Commission's counts of names left off the draft rolls.
claims.site: The states' own figures count 13,39,03,307 names left off the drafts in 31 states. Of them 2,79,69,558 were entered as dead, 9,56,35,923 as shifted, absent or another reason, and 1,01,48,459 as duplicates.
claims.stops: These are the reasons the officers wrote down, and the rolls do not show whether they were right.

claims.quote: In fact, ground reports from several states (including a careful state-wide survey in Rajasthan) suggest that majority of ASDD deletions are legitimate.
claims.rests: It rests on ground reports and a state-wide survey in Rajasthan, which the column does not name.
claims.site: No such survey is part of these figures. Rajasthan's press note gives 4,61,159 names left off as dead, 12,91,846 as shifted, 2,46,249 as absent and 1,53,617 as duplicates.
claims.stops: A reason says what an officer wrote down. Whether it was right needs a check at the door, which the rolls cannot give.

claims.quote: In India as a whole, the shortfall is as large as 15% (see table). The gap shrinks when final lists are prepared, but not much.
claims.rests: It rests on his table. All major states held 85 per cent of projected adults in the draft, and the twelve states with final lists 86 per cent in the draft and 88 per cent in the final lists.
claims.site: Across the 19 states the drafts held 80,65,69,819 names, 84.4 per cent of projected adults. In the twelve with final rolls the drafts held 85.7 per cent and the final rolls 87.5 per cent, or 88.4 per cent with West Bengal's 60,06,675 names under adjudication counted on the roll.
claims.stops: His table covers the major states only, so the 15 per cent describes those states.

claims.quote: Pre-SIR lists were, in fact, far from inclusive. A significant fraction of the adult population was left out - up to 10% perhaps, judging from patchy evidence.
claims.rests: It rests on what he calls patchy evidence, which the column does not set out.
claims.site: Before the revision six of the 19 states held more names than projected adults, which fits his account of surplus names on the rolls.
claims.stops: The rolls cannot show how many adults were never on them, so the 10 per cent cannot be checked here.

claims.quote: When a migrant worker is marked as 'Shifted', the largest category in ASDD lists, in their village of origin, there is no guarantee that they have been, or will be, enrolled at the destination point.
claims.kind: A fact about how the revision was run
claims.rests: It rests on the reasons officers gave for names left off the drafts.
claims.site: Shifted is the largest single reason in Uttar Pradesh (1,29,77,472, 44.9 per cent of names left off), Gujarat (54.6 per cent), Rajasthan (12,91,846) and Bihar (26,55,900 against 22,32,586 dead). In West Bengal more names were entered as dead (24,16,852) than as shifted (19,88,076). Most states publish shifted, absent and other reasons together.
claims.stops: The rolls do not show whether a person entered as shifted has enrolled where they moved.

claims.quote: When the SIR exercise began in June 2025, the most important task was not to weed out surplus names but to include those left out in pre-SIR lists.

strongest: His figures agree with the official figures for the same states to the rounding he prints. Across the 19 states with projected adults, the rolls before the revision held 98.3 per cent and the drafts 84.4 per cent, against his 99 and 85. In the twelve states with final rolls the official figures give 97.3, 85.7 and 87.5 per cent against his 97, 86 and 88, and 88.4 per cent when West Bengal's 60,06,675 names under adjudication are counted on the roll.
He separates the gap by stage, and he says plainly that most names left off as absent, shifted, dead or duplicate may have been left off rightly.
His account of surplus names fits the six states whose rolls held more names than projected adults before the revision.
further: The 12 crore is the joint column's extrapolation from nine states to the whole country, and his table gives no final figure for all major states.
The 10 per cent of adults missing before the revision rests on evidence he calls patchy and does not set out.
He calls shifted the largest category. It is the largest single reason in Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat, Rajasthan and Bihar, and in West Bengal more names were entered as dead.
The 15 per cent he gives for India as a whole is his table's figure for the major states, without Assam and Himachal Pradesh.

people.name: Jean Drèze and Yogendra Yadav
people.role: Jean Drèze is a visiting professor in the Department of Economics at Ranchi University. Yogendra Yadav is a member of Swaraj India and national convenor of Bharat Jodo Abhiyan, and has his own panel on this page. Drèze's follow-up column of 21 October has a panel of its own.
people.intro: The quotations are from their joint column in The Indian Express of 20 October 2026, a reply to Surjit Bhalla. They set each state's final roll against its projected adult population and count the whole gap as missing voters. The print edition carries a table for nine states that the online text leaves out.

pieces.title: Let’s not be in denial — disenfranchisement in real

claims.quote: We can compare the size of the post-SIR voter lists with official estimates of the adult population that is eligible to vote. Indeed, the ECI itself has been using these population estimates as a benchmark to evaluate its voter lists.
claims.rests: It rests on the Technical Group's projections of adults in early 2026, set against the final rolls.
claims.site: The All India page uses the same projections and makes the same comparison. Their adults equal the projection on the All India page for all nine states, 60,12,56,000 together. Before the revision those states' rolls held 97.5 per cent of projected adults.
claims.stops: A projection counts residents. It counts migrant workers where they live and adults who are not citizens, and it has not been checked against a count since 2011.

claims.quote: For these nine states combined, the voter list falls short of the adult population by more than 7 crore. Almost 12 per cent of the adult population is excluded.
claims.rests: It rests on their table in the print edition, 601.2 million projected adults against 530.6 million on the final rolls.
claims.site: Eight of their nine final lists equal the official final rolls. West Bengal's 70.5 million is the Chief Electoral Officer's final roll of 28 February 2026, 6,44,52,609, plus all 60,06,675 names then held for adjudication. Of those, 27,16,393 were later found not eligible, and the roll the 2026 election was held on held 6,82,51,008. So their own method understates West Bengal, 8.4 per cent short where the election roll gives 11.4 and the final roll 16.3. On the official figures the nine final rolls hold 52,45,53,415 names, 7.67 crore or 12.8 per cent short of projected adults, and 7.29 crore or 12.1 per cent with West Bengal on the election roll.
claims.stops: The gap counts people wrongly left off together with adults who were never on the roll, and the rolls cannot separate the two.

claims.quote: In Uttar Pradesh alone, 2.8 crore are excluded —more than 17 per cent of the adult population.
claims.rests: It rests on their table, 161.7 million adults against 134 million on Uttar Pradesh's final roll.
claims.site: The official figures bear this out. Uttar Pradesh's final roll of 10 April 2026 holds 13,39,84,792 names against 16,16,85,000 projected adults, 2.77 crore or 17.1 per cent short. Before the revision its roll held 95.5 per cent of projected adults. Gujarat's gap is about as large, 17.4 per cent, and Gujarat draws migrant workers whom the projection counts where they live.
claims.stops: A projection counts residents, so a state's gap moves with how many of its adults live elsewhere and where they are registered.

claims.quote: If the average exclusion rate of 12 per cent for these nine states is representative of the whole country, then the total number of excluded adults or “missing voters” would be around 12 crore.
claims.rests: It rests on applying the nine states' rate to the whole country.
claims.site: Twelve per cent of 101.6 crore is 12.2 crore, as they say, and they state the condition. The nine states hold about 63 per cent of the projected adults in the 19 states with projections. Across those 19 states the drafts held 84.4 per cent of projected adults. In the 22 states with a final roll, the rise between draft and final came to 14.6 per cent of the names left off. That rise counts new voters too, so at most that share of the names was put back.
claims.stops: Ten states have no final roll yet, so no national count of adults off the final rolls can be given.

claims.quote: Assuming that these draft lists will undergo the same level of corrections as the first two phases, Rahul Shastri estimates that the final post-SIR voter list for the entire country will be around 87.8 crore. (This estimate does not take into account any corrective action the ECI may undertake from now on to undo the damage). Compare this to India’s current adult population of about 101.6 crore. We are staring at a staggering figure of about 14 crore “missing voters” — adult Indians eligible to vote but excluded from the final electoral rolls.
claims.rests: It rests on Rahul Shastri's estimate of the final rolls for the whole country, from the phase III drafts, against 101.6 crore adults.
claims.site: Their 101.6 less 87.8 is 13.8 crore. Across the 31 states with a draft, 13,39,03,307 names were left off, which left about 81.7 crore on the drafts before claims were heard and before Assam, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh are added. An estimate of 87.8 crore for the final rolls sits within what those figures allow. Their adult total is close to the UN's 1,01,76,59,624 for mid-2024.
claims.stops: It projects final rolls that are not yet published, and the estimate itself is not set out in the column.

claims.quote: These disenfranchised voters comprise those eligible voters who featured on the pre-SIR list and were wrongfully removed during the SIR, as well as persons who should have been added to the voter list but were not.

Voluntary non-registration is not seen as a common phenomenon by the media, political parties or the ECI. Second, voter registration in India has been state initiated. Therefore, non-registration is a failure of the electoral officials that can be rectified, rather than a shortfall to be accepted.
claims.kind: A fact about how the revision was run
claims.rests: It rests on their reading of how registration works in India.
claims.site: The law supports both readings. Section 23 of the 1950 Act lets a person who is not on the roll apply to be included, which is Bhalla's point. In an intensive revision the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960 have the roll prepared afresh, and the revision ordered on 24 June 2025 carried a form to every elector on the old roll, which is theirs.
claims.stops: No published figure measures how many adults choose not to register.

claims.quote: Indeed, in some earlier years, the enrolment gap among the young was much lower than 7.5 per cent — for example, it was 5.2 per cent of the total adult population in 2014.
claims.rests: It rests on a count of young adults off the 2014 roll. The column gives no source.
claims.site: No roll by age has been found. Its series of rolls against the UN's estimate of adults shows the roll closer to the adult population in 2014, 98.2 per 100, than in 2024, 96.3, which fits a smaller gap among the young then.
claims.stops: The 5.2 per cent itself cannot be checked against the official figures.

claims.quote: Even if we were to accept Bhalla’s inflated benchmark of 8.5 per cent for voluntary non-registration, there would still be 14 million unfairly excluded voters in Uttar Pradesh alone. This clearly jars with Bhalla’s claim that only 7 million were excluded in the nine states combined.
claims.rests: It rests on Uttar Pradesh's adults less Bhalla's 8.5 per cent, set against its final roll.
claims.site: The arithmetic holds. At 91.5 per cent of 16,16,85,000 projected adults the clean roll is 14,79,41,775, and the final roll of 13,39,84,792 is 1,39,56,983 short of it. Bhalla's 70 lakh is reached another way. He uses his own count of adults, about 1.1 crore below the projection for these nine states and 15.9 crore for Uttar Pradesh, sets each state's allowance from its own registration of the young, 60 per cent in Uttar Pradesh, and nets states with surplus names against states that fall short. With a flat 8.5 per cent in every state the nine final rolls are about 1.25 crore short after netting on his count of adults, and about 2.6 crore on the projection.
claims.stops: Which allowance is right depends on how many young adults chose not to register, and no published figure measures that.

strongest: Their method is the one on the All India page, final rolls against the Technical Group's projected adults, and eight of their nine state figures match the official ones.
Their Uttar Pradesh arithmetic holds on Bhalla's own benchmark, 1.40 crore short at 91.5 per cent of adults.
They say plainly that the gap counts people wrongly left off together with adults who were never enrolled.

The rolls before the revision bear on their side. In the same nine states they held 97.5 per cent of projected adults, more than a normal shortfall of 8.5 per cent allows unless many names on them belonged to people who had died, moved or been entered twice.
further: They call the whole gap excluded or missing voters. It includes adults who were never on the roll, and a projection counts residents, migrants where they live and adults who are not citizens.
The national 12 and 14 crore are extrapolations, the second from another analyst's estimate of final rolls not yet published.
Tamil Nadu and Kerala held more names than projected adults before the revision, so part of their falls was names that should not have been on the roll.
Their West Bengal figure counts the 27 lakh later found not eligible as still on the roll, which makes West Bengal's gap look smaller than their own method gives.

people.name: P. Chidambaram
people.role: Member of the Rajya Sabha for the Congress and a former Union Minister of Finance and of Home Affairs.
people.intro: The quotations come from one post of his on X, of 16 October 2026. He wrote it the morning after the Commission ordered a special summary revision of the rolls in 17 states and union territories, and the Supreme Court issued notice on the INDIA bloc leaders' petition against the Commission. The News Mill carried the whole post the same day, with inputs from ANI.

pieces.title: After the protests and the notice issued by the Supreme Court, wisdom has dawned on the ECI and Mr Gyanesh Kumar ...

claims.quote: After the protests and the notice issued by the Supreme Court, wisdom has dawned on the ECI and Mr Gyanesh Kumar
claims.rests: It rests on the order for a special summary revision, as ANI and PTI reported it on 15 October 2026, and the Supreme Court's notice of the same day on the INDIA bloc leaders' petition.
claims.site: Both events are real and fell on the same day. None of the reports of the order (ANI, PTI as carried by Siasat, and The News Mill) gives a reason tied to the protests or the notice. The order covers the 17 states and union territories where the revision is over, with Assam, which had a Special Revision, so it stops nothing that was running. The Commission had already said on 26 September 2026, before both notices, that the revision was complete in 20 states and union territories, and it ordered a drive to enrol people left out.
claims.stops: The rolls and the Commission's letter give no reason for its timing, and the figures make no claim about why the Commission acted.

claims.quote: S.I.R. has been abandoned for the 17 remaining States and UTs, and it will only be the customary SSR (special summary revision)
claims.kind: A fact about how the revision was run
claims.rests: It rests on the Commission's letter No. 23/2026-ERS of 15 October 2026 ordering a special summary revision with 1 January 2027 as the qualifying date, as published by the Chief Electoral Officer of Kerala, and as ANI and PTI (through Siasat) reported it.
claims.site: The number 17 is the order's. The 17 are the states and union territories where the revision is over, with Assam, which had a Special Revision instead. All 16 others have a final roll, the latest Punjab's of 12 October 2026. PTI's copy says that in these 17 states the special intensive revision is over and calls the summary revision annual. For the states still in the revision, ANI reports that the schedule will be announced separately, and no report or document found says the revision has stopped anywhere. On 24 October 2026 ten states and union territories were still in it, nine awaiting a final roll and Tripura with no draft yet. The Commission's letter of 15 October 2026 names 16 states and union territories where the revision is going on or has just been completed, among them six that have finished (Odisha, Arunachal Pradesh, Sikkim, Mizoram, Chandigarh, and Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu), and says their summary revision will be scheduled later.
claims.stops: No copy of the order and no schedule for a summary revision in the states still in the revision has been found.

claims.quote: Documents to prove citizenship need not be produced
claims.kind: A fact about how the revision was run
claims.rests: It rests on his reading of the change to a summary revision. He names no document, and no report of the order mentions documents of citizenship.
claims.site: The documents point the same way for new applicants. In the revision a declaration went with every Form 6, first the Bihar declaration of 24 June 2025 with its documents by year of birth, then the declaration of 27 October 2025, which asks for an entry in the roll of the state's last intensive revision. The Commission said on 26 September 2026 that outside the revision the forms of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960 apply. PTI reports there will be no house-to-house visits in the summary revision. The revision did not ask every elector for documents either. From its second phase none were collected with the enumeration form, and notices went to those who could not be linked to the old roll.
claims.stops: The Commission's letter of 15 October 2026 says nothing about documents, and no instruction on what a Form 6 applicant must file in the summary revision has been found.

claims.quote: Why were 20 States discriminated against under S.I.R.
and 13,30,00,000 names (including the dead) were removed without Due Process?
claims.rests: It rests on a count of the names left off the draft rolls in the revision. He gives no source.
claims.site: Across the 31 states with a draft roll, 13,39,03,307 names were left off the drafts, 14.08 per 100 of the 95,08,13,771 on the rolls before. His 13.30 crore is about 9 lakh below that. Of those names, 2,79,69,558, about one in five, were entered as dead, as he says. The 20 states finished by 26 September 2026 account for 7,48,54,691, and the other 5.9 crore are in 11 states that had not finished by then, nine of which were still awaiting a final roll on 24 October 2026. A name left off the draft has not been deleted. The Supreme Court held for Bihar that leaving a name off the draft “is not tantamount to a final deletion, but is only a provisional step”. Deletion is an order of the registration officer under section 22 of the 1950 Act, after a reasonable opportunity of being heard, with an appeal under section 24. After the draft, 33,65,116 names were deleted in the 20 states that published those figures. On Bihar the Court held that the deletions were not contrary to the procedure of Rule 21A and that the safeguards of notice and hearing were preserved in substance.
claims.stops: The figures count names. It cannot say whether a hearing was given in any case, or how many of those left off were entitled to stay. The Court's judgment is on Bihar, and the later phases are before it in petitions now pending.

claims.quote: After removing crores of names illegally, now the ECI has undertaken another exercise to include the 'left out' voters!
claims.kind: A fact about how the revision was run
claims.rests: It rests on the drive for electors left out, announced on 26 September 2026 and set out in the Commission's letter of 1 October, and the summary revision ordered on 15 October.
claims.site: The drive exists. On 26 September the Commission said anyone whose name had been left out during the revision or after may apply, and told its officers to launch a special drive to enrol them. The letter of 1 October tells booth officers to compare the roll from before the revision with the current one, visit those missing and help those found eligible fill in Form 6. In the 22 states with a final roll, the roll rose by 1,13,76,238 on net between draft and final. That is at most 14.6% of the names left off there, and the rise counts new voters too.
claims.stops: No count of Form 6 applications from the drive has been found. The word illegally is his. The one judgment so far, on Bihar, held the deletions there within the procedure of the Rules, and the later phases have not been ruled on.

claims.quote: Mr Gyanesh Kumar should be surcharged for the double expenditure

strongest: His 20 is the Commission's own count of states and union territories where the revision was complete on 26 September 2026, and the states' own records give the same 20 on that date.
His 13.30 crore is within one per cent of the 13,39,03,307 names left off the drafts in 31 states, and about one in five of them were entered as dead, as he says.
The Commission did order a drive to bring back people left out, on 26 September and 1 October 2026, and has now ordered a summary revision with the same aim.
Outside the revision the Commission said the forms of the Rules apply, so the declaration the revision attached to Form 6 should not go with one in the summary revision.
further: The 17 states in the order are where the revision is over. The letter says the summary revision in the states still in it will be scheduled later, and nothing found says the revision has been abandoned anywhere.
The Commission's letter gives no reason, and the drive for people left out was ordered on 26 September, before both notices. Why the Commission acted is his reading.

He sets 13.30 crore against 20 states. Those 20 account for 7.49 crore, and the rest are in 11 states that had not finished by 26 September, nine of which were still awaiting a final roll on 24 October 2026.

Names left off the draft have not been deleted, and the Supreme Court held Bihar's deletions consistent with the procedure of the Rules. “Without Due Process” and “illegally” are his charges, and no court has ruled on them for the later phases.
No report of the order says documents of citizenship need not be produced. That is his inference, though the Commission's note of 26 September points the same way for new applicants.

people.name: Abhijeet Dipke
people.role: Founder of the Cockroach Janta Party, which has led protests in Mumbai and Delhi since 2 October 2026 calling for the Chief Election Commissioner to resign.
people.intro: The quotations come from his press conference at the Press Club of India in New Delhi on 15 October 2026, held with AISA's Neha Bora the day before the party's march at Connaught Place, as PTI reported it, and from an earlier press conference on 24 September 2026 as Business Today reported it. The party's own recording is on YouTube. PTI's Hindi service rendered his word 'setting' as मिलीभगत (collusion), and which language he spoke in is not recorded.

pieces.title: CJP to hold Tiranga march at Connaught Place amid security curbs
'If Gyanesh Kumar doesn't resign in 48 hours...': CJP's Abhijeet Dipke warns of nationwide protest

claims.quote: The margin of victory in 2024 was just 2 per cent. Over 13 crore voters deleted — around 14 percent.
claims.rests: It rests on the Commission's counts of names left off the drafts, set against the national gap in vote share between the two alliances in 2024. In the same report PTI put the NDA at around 43 per cent of the 2024 vote and the INDIA bloc at around 40.6 per cent.
claims.site: Across the 31 states with a draft roll, 13,39,03,307 names were left off the drafts, 14.08 per 100 of the 95,08,13,771 on the rolls before. By the reason recorded beside each, 2,79,69,558 (20.9%) were entered as dead, 1,01,48,459 (7.6%) as duplicates and 9,56,35,923 (71.5%) as shifted, absent or other. His 14 per cent is right to the precision he gives. In the 22 states whose final rolls are out, 7,77,48,303 names were left off of 65,67,36,949 (11.84 per 100), and the net rise after the draft brought back at most 14.6% of them.
claims.stops: A reason is what the officer wrote down, and nobody checked it. No party vote shares are held here, so his 2 per cent is not checked. The 2024 election was held on the rolls from before the revision, which was ordered on 24 June 2025, so the names left off had no part in the 2024 result.

claims.quote: Where 2 per cent is deciding the election, you are deleting 13 crore votes. What is this if not a setting?
claims.rests: It rests on the size of the count against a national gap in vote share. He offers no other evidence of purpose.
claims.site: Elections are decided seat by seat. Spread evenly over each state's Lok Sabha seats, the names left off exceed the 2024 winning margin in 373 of 516 seats in those 31 states, and 115 of the 542 contested seats were won by fewer than 50,000 votes. The even spread is an assumption, and in Tamil Nadu it gives 27 seats over the margin against 19 counted seat by seat. In Bihar the names left off came more from booths that voted NDA in 2024 (49.0% against 37.8% INDIA), and the estimate there is that 4 to 6 seats change hands, in both directions.
claims.stops: The rolls record names and reasons. They cannot show why anything was done, and the figures make no claim about purpose.

claims.quote: In total, more than 13 crore votes have been deleted. This is not a small number.
claims.rests: It rests on the Commission's counts of names left off the drafts, as he gave them on 24 September 2026.
claims.site: Across the 31 states with a draft roll, 13,39,03,307 names were left off the drafts, 14.08 per 100 of the 95,08,13,771 on the rolls before. By the reason recorded beside each, 2,79,69,558 (20.9%) were entered as dead, 1,01,48,459 (7.6%) as duplicates and 9,56,35,923 (71.5%) as shifted, absent or other.
claims.stops: These are names left off the drafts, and some came back afterwards. Most were never votes cast, since the count includes the dead and duplicate entries and the roll holds people who do not vote.

claims.quote: Pinarayi Vijayan would have won, but due to the deletion of votes in Kerala, he did not become the Chief Minister.
claims.kind: A reading of the effect on results
claims.rests: No figures are given in the report, which adds that he provided no evidence for the claim.
claims.site: Kerala's Chief Electoral Officer published no table of names left off. Measured as the fall in the roll from January 2025, the roll fell by 6,67,990 by the election (2.40 per 100), and that fall was larger than the winning margin in 38 of 140 seats, or 30 when taken at each seat's turnout. In Dharmadam, his own seat, the roll at the election was larger than in January 2025, 2,06,000 against 1,98,819, and the CPI(M) held the seat by 19,247.
claims.stops: A fall larger than a margin shows that it could have decided a seat, never that it did. No model of how those left off would have voted in Kerala has been made.

strongest: His count is right. 13,39,03,307 names were left off the drafts, 14.08 per 100 on the rolls before.
The names left off are large against close seat margins, which is the strongest form of his point.
further: The 2024 election came before the revision, so the names left off could not have shaped its margin. The comparison works as a warning about the next election.

The 13 crore are names left off the drafts by recorded reason, among them the dead and duplicate entries, and some came back on the final rolls. Calling them votes deleted goes further than the figures.

A national gap in vote share is a share of votes cast, and the names left off are a share of the roll. Seats are the measure that decides results, and the seat figures here show the names left off large enough to decide many seats, never that they did.
Setting is a claim about purpose, which the rolls cannot show. In Bihar, the one state where the effect has been modelled, it runs both ways.
The Kerala claim goes further than the fall in the roll. Dharmadam's roll grew, and the CPI(M) held the seat.

people.name: The Reporters' Collective and the Chief Electoral Officer of Uttar Pradesh
people.role: The Reporters' Collective is an investigative newsroom that has reported on the SIR in several states. Navdeep Rinwa is the Chief Electoral Officer of Uttar Pradesh, the official responsible for the state's electoral roll.
people.intro: The Collective reported on 9 October 2026 that the Commission's software produced 85,854 objections to delete Uttar Pradesh electors with no reason given, and followed it on 14 October with the Chief Electoral Officer's answers. This panel sets the two reports beside his answers, as the Collective and IANS printed them, beside his February count, and beside the Commission's order of 9 October capping objections as the press reported it. The Chief Electoral Officer's video and his first post on X could not be found, so his words are given as those outlets printed them.

pieces.title: In UP SIR, ECI Software Auto-generated 85,854 Forms to Delete Voters Without a Reason
pieces.outlet: The Reporters' Collective (Sumedha Mittal, Ayushi Kar, Shubhangi Derhgawen)

pieces.title: UP CEO Admits ECI Auto-generated 85,000+ Voter Deletion Forms Without a Reason, Confirms Mass Deletion Attempts Against Muslims
pieces.outlet: The Reporters' Collective (Sumedha Mittal, Ayushi Kar)

pieces.title: 85,854 फॉर्म-7 स्वतः तैयार कर मतदाताओं के नाम काटने का दावा भ्रामक: यूपी चुनाव आयोग
pieces.title_en: Claim that names were cut by preparing 85,854 Form 7s automatically is misleading: UP election office

pieces.title: 'No mass deletion as claimed': Only 4,336 names removed via 3rd party Form 7 in SIR 2026, says UP chief electoral officer
To curb misuse, EC caps 10 objection forms per person seeking voter removal from electoral rolls

claims.quote: Our analysis of the data scraped from the ECI’s website shows that 85,854 (98.5 percent) of the 87,127 requests filed by EROs and AEROs have no reason mentioned for deletion.
claims.rests: It rests on the Collective's own scrape of the Form 7s shown on the Chief Electoral Officer's website. The scraped file is not published.
claims.site: Uttar Pradesh's draft of 6 January 2026 left off 2,88,74,067 of the 15,44,30,092 names on the roll before it. After the draft, 8,15,996 names were deleted, as the press reported the Chief Electoral Officer's figures, and 3,50,026 of them were people who did not answer a notice. The Chief Electoral Officer's figures count 2,68,682 Form 7s filed from 6 January to 6 March 2026.
claims.stops: No count of Form 7s after 6 March and none of forms filed by officers has been found, so the 85,854 cannot be checked. How many of the 8,15,996 deletions went through a Form 7 has not been published.

claims.quote: But the officers did not fill the forms. The ECI’s own software, ERONET automatically generated these forms, when officials deleted voters during the SIR hearings. The auto-generated forms came loaded with the officers’ digital signatures and were sent up for approval by their seniors.
claims.kind: A fact about how the revision was run
claims.rests: It rests on interviews with four election officials whom the Collective does not name, and the pattern in its scraped forms. No document from the software is published.
claims.site: Notices went to 3.26 crore of the electors on the draft, 1.04 crore with no link to the old roll and 2.22 crore for discrepancies, as the Chief Electoral Officer told The Times of India. Of those deleted after the draft, 3,50,026 had not answered their notice. The Chief Electoral Officer's office has said that notices, hearings and orders came before every deletion, and it has not denied that the software produced the forms.
claims.stops: No record of how ERONET works or of who signed which form is public.

claims.quote: In our investigation, we also found that a total of 1,10,476 voter deletion requests were submitted by individuals and accepted by the ECI after the legally mandated deadline.
claims.rests: It rests on the same scrape, read against the end of the claims and objections period. The report does not say which date it took as the deadline, and the likeliest is 6 March 2026.
claims.site: The count of Form 7s in Uttar Pradesh is 2,68,682, from 6 January to 6 March 2026. The final roll came on 10 April 2026 with 13,39,84,792 electors.
claims.stops: No record shows which Form 7s were filed late or what became of them.

claims.quote: Yet, in his video, Rinwa confirmed our finding that the ECI software had forced election officers in UP to sign 85,854 forms to delete voters without stating a reason.

“The total number of names against which [bulk] deletion complaints were made through these Form 7s was only about 4,700. In Uttar Pradesh, which has a population in crores and where we have 13.39 crore [voters]. They found only 4,700 such names where there were multiple Form 7s,” said Rinwa.
claims.rests: It rests on his own count of names that drew more than one Form 7, with no source given. The words are from his recorded video of 9 October 2026 as the Collective quotes them, and the video could not be found.
claims.site: His 13.39 crore is the final roll, 13,39,84,792 electors. The Collective sets his 4,700 against its finding of more than 200 attempts to delete names in bulk across the state, which were objections filed by individuals and are a separate matter from the 85,854 forms. In February he gave 4,336 deletions from objections filed by other people, which counts deletions where this counts names objected to.
claims.stops: No count of names that drew more than one Form 7 has been found.

claims.quote: यूपी एसआईआर में 85,854 फार्म-7 स्वतः बनाकर बिना कारण मतदाताओं के नाम हटाने का दावा भ्रामक है। संबंधित मामलों में नोटिस, सुनवाई, जांच और आदेश के बाद कार्रवाई हुई। 6 मार्च के बाद लंबित मामलों पर निर्णय भी नियमानुसार हुए। सही जानकारी के लिए आधिकारिक स्रोतों पर भरोसा करें।
claims.translation: "Claims that 85,854 Form-7 entries were auto-generated to delete UP voters without reason during SIR are misleading. Notices, hearings, scrutiny and recorded orders preceded action. Pending cases were decided after 6 March as per procedure." (IANS's English, The Hans India, 13 Oct 2026, which omits the last sentence, 'Rely on official sources for correct information'.)
claims.kind: A fact about how the revision was run
claims.rests: It rests on the office's account of its own procedure, with no figures. IANS reported it from Lucknow on Tuesday 13 October 2026. The Collective describes an earlier post on X, minutes after its report of 9 October, which used different words, and that post could not be found.
claims.site: The statement answers how the forms were described and gives no count of them. After the draft, 8,15,996 names were deleted, as the press reported the office's figures. Of these, 3,50,026 did not answer a notice, 3,28,960 were entered as shifted, 79,076 as multiple entries, 55,865 as dead and 2,069 as under age or not citizens.
claims.stops: The office has not published how many of those deletions went through a Form 7 and how many through a notice, so the split is unknown.

claims.quote: “Against a total of 12.55 crore voters during the claims and objections period (Jan 6–Feb 16), only 23,935 names have been deleted so far,” he said.
claims.rests: It rests on his running count to 16 February 2026, eight weeks before the final roll, as The Times of India quotes him.
claims.site: The draft held 12,55,56,025 electors. By the final roll, 8,15,996 names had been deleted after the draft, as the press reported his office's figures.
claims.stops: The end figure is known only as the press reported it, and nothing is known between February and April.

claims.quote: During the special period designated for filing claims and objections – typically known as the Summary Revision period – an individual voter is allowed to submit a maximum of 10 Form 7 applications.
claims.kind: A fact about how the revision was run
claims.rests: It rests on PTI's account of the Commission's letter of 9 October 2026 to Chief Electoral Officers. News On AIR, Deccan Herald, Deccan Chronicle, DT Next and Outlook report the same limit. None of them prints the letter, and it could not be found.
claims.site: Every report of the order found gives 10 objections per elector during a claims period and five a month at other times. The Collective's report of 14 October says the order allowed no more than 30 objections a month, which matches no other report and cites no document.
claims.stops: No count of Form 7s per objector has been found.

strongest: The count comes from the Chief Electoral Officer's own published forms, with a stated denominator (85,854 of 87,127) and dates, so anyone with the same pages could repeat it.
The Chief Electoral Officer's office answered how the forms were described, and no report found has it disputing the number.
further: The Collective writes that he confirmed its finding. That rests on what he did not say in the video, since it quotes no sentence in which he confirms the count.
The limit of 30 objections a month in the follow-up matches no other report of the Commission's order, all of which give 10 per elector during a claims period and five a month afterwards.
The account of how the software produced the forms rests on four officials the Collective does not name.

people.name: Rahul Gandhi
people.role: Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha and a Congress MP, who has led his party's campaign against the revision since the Voter Adhikar Yatra in Bihar in 2025.
people.intro: The quotations come from four pieces. They are a post on his WhatsApp channel in August 2025 as PTI translated it, his press briefing in Delhi on 24 September 2026, his post on X of 5 October 2026, and the joint petition of INDIA bloc leaders to the Supreme Court as The Indian Express quoted it on 13 October 2026.

pieces.title: SIR is 'new weapon' of 'vote chori', will protect 'one person, one vote', says Rahul Gandhi
LoP Rahul Gandhi addresses Delhi press briefing amid ECI dissent row over SIR
Gyanesh Kumar changed Form 6 'illegally' during SIR, says Rahul Gandhi
Opposition to Supreme Court: Probe Election Commission decisions, audit of SIR voter deletions

claims.quote: SIR is a new weapon of vote theft. Coincidentally, these people standing with me in this picture are 'living' proof of this theft. ... All of them had cast their vote in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections - but by the time Bihar assembly elections came, their identity, their existence was erased from the democracy of India
claims.translation: PTI's translation from his Hindi post; The Hindu adds, in reported speech, that he said the collusion of the BJP and the Commission 'is punishing them for being Bahujan and poor'.
claims.rests: He rests the claim on six people from Bihar he met at Sasaram on 17 August 2025, who he says voted in 2024 and were missing from the draft roll. The quotation is PTI's English translation of his Hindi post, and the line about Bahujan and poor voters being punished is PTI's reported speech. The six cases have not been checked against a record.
claims.site: Bihar's phase 1 lists left 65,59,626 names off the draft. The lists record no caste, so caste is guessed from surnames in two ways, and the two point in different directions. In the first, Scheduled Castes were 20.0 per cent of the classified names left off against 19.65 per cent in the 2023 caste survey, and General names 34.4 per cent against 10.72. In the second, Scheduled Castes were 30.0 per cent and Muslim names 29.0 per cent. One group the lists do count was over-represented. Women were 55.5 per cent of those left off against 47.9 per cent of the roll.
claims.stops: Caste guessed from names is no identification, and the bounds on every group are wide. No record of income exists for those left off, so nothing shows whether they were poorer than other electors. It says nothing about what anyone intended.

claims.quote: let me tell you there is already more than enough information to make this a 100% certainty, not 99%, a 100% certainty that Indian elections, Lok Sabha elections, 2024 election, Vidhan Sabha elections, are all being rigged.
claims.kind: A reading of the effect on results
claims.rests: He points to his earlier presentations on Maharashtra, Mahadevapura, Aland and Haryana and to information he says came from inside the Commission. The briefing sets out no figure behind the certainty.
claims.site: Bihar 2025 is the one election after a revision that has been modelled here. More names were left off the draft than the winning margin in 174 of 243 seats, and the net fall to the final roll exceeded the margin in 124. Estimating how the electors left off or deleted would have voted moves 4 to 6 seats, some each way, and the NDA keeps its majority on every estimate. A model of the swing that allows for each seat's 2020 lead gives a slope of +0.31, with a range from -0.27 to +0.89, which takes in no effect at all.
claims.stops: A count of names left off or deleted above the margin shows that they were large enough to decide a seat. It cannot show that they did. The 2024 Lok Sabha election came before the revision, and no evidence on changes to the roll before it is at hand.

claims.quote: Please understand what these two gentlemen are saying. They're saying that the vote does not exist in India anymore.
claims.rests: He refers to the Express investigation of 23 September 2026 into the two Election Commissioners' notes. The paper reports 14 objections, about Form 6, deletions and restorations, appeals in West Bengal and access to the roll software. It does not report either Commissioner saying the vote no longer exists.
claims.site: The section Inside the Commission on the process page lists each dated objection as the paper reported it. Among them are a note of 16 May 2026 that Form 6 cannot be changed without amending the 1960 Rules and a note of 13 August calling the change unauthorised and illegal.
claims.stops: Only the paper's account of the notes is public. His sentence is his own reading of them.

claims.quote: SIR came once we started saying there's a problem with voter deletion and addition it was a response to our questions and the idea was let us broad brush this and clean this thing out because we're going to get into trouble.
claims.rests: He gives his own account of the order of events and cites no document. The quotation is from the questions near the end of the briefing.
claims.site: The order of 24 June 2025 directed a Special Intensive Revision in the entire country, starting with Bihar. The joint petition he later signed alleges that no recorded decision of the full Commission authorised the nationwide revision. The Commission's press note 120 of 26 September 2026 says the order had its unanimous approval.
claims.stops: No document says why the revision was ordered. It holds the order and the two competing accounts of how it was approved.

claims.quote: It is now established beyond doubt that Gyanesh Kumar changed Form 6 illegally and unilaterally. This is just one more proof of him abusing his position to help the BJP. He and everyone else involved in this criminal assault on our democracy will be held accountable
claims.kind: A fact about how the revision was run
claims.rests: His post of 5 October 2026 cites no document. It follows his post of 1 October, which cites the Commissioners' recorded objections as the Express reported them, and it came after the Supreme Court's remark of 5 October that it had not approved any modified Form 6.
claims.site: The Disputes page carries each step. The Express reported the declaration on the online Form 6 on 12 July 2026, and two Commissioners objected to it in writing. On 5 October the Chief Justice said in court that any modified Form 6 had not been approved by the Court. On 12 October the bench said this meant only that the new form did not exist when the Bihar case was heard, and that the Court had neither approved nor disapproved it. The Commission's press note 120 says the full Commission approved the declaration and kept it for the revision, and by 30 September it had been taken off the online form in states whose final roll was out.
claims.stops: No court has decided whether the change was lawful. No document says who made it, and the Commission says all its decisions were unanimous. That it was done to help the BJP is his inference, and the records show nothing about purpose.

claims.quote: reportedly reflected a reduction of approximately 20.66 lakh names from the electorate of about 2.14 crore recorded in June 2026
claims.rests: These are the words of the joint writ petition filed on 12 October 2026 by INDIA bloc leaders, the bloc's petition, signed by him among others, as The Indian Express quotes it. The petition says reportedly, and rests on press reports of Punjab's figures.
claims.site: The figure matches the official count. Punjab's roll before the revision held 2,14,61,043 names and 20,66,635 were left off, 9.63 for every 100 electors. Of those, 5,74,568 were entered as dead, 13,56,846 as shifted, absent or other and 1,19,145 as duplicates. After the draft 7,97,263 names were added and 86,038 deleted, and the final roll of 12 October 2026 holds 2,01,00,727, a net fall of 13,60,316, or 6.34 for every 100.
claims.stops: Punjab's figures came through the press, given at the end of enumeration before the draft, and the published final-roll figures do not add up exactly. The rise after the draft counts new voters too, so it cannot be called names put back.

strongest: The Punjab figure in the bloc's petition matches the official count.

On Form 6 his account of the record holds. Two Commissioners objected in writing, and the declaration was later taken off the online form in states whose final roll was out. On 5 October the Supreme Court said it had approved no modified form, and on 12 October it said it had neither approved nor disapproved one.
In Bihar more names were left off the draft than the winning margin in 174 of 243 seats, so exclusions large enough to decide a result were present.
further: He says it is certain that the 2024 and later elections were rigged. The one model here of an election after a revision, for Bihar, finds 4 to 6 seats moving, some each way, and no change of majority.
He reads the exclusions as falling on Bahujan and poor voters. The lists record neither caste nor income, and the two guesses at caste from names disagree.
He attributes a purpose to the Commission and to the Form 6 change, which the records cannot show.

people.name: Prannoy Roy
people.role: Psephologist and journalist, a founder of NDTV, who now presents DeKoder.
people.intro: In a seven-minute episode on 8 October 2026 he sets the names West Bengal left off or deleted beside the swing against the TMC, and sets the women and the Muslim electors among them beside their shares of the roll.

pieces.title: More SIR Deletions, Bigger BJP Swing? Prannoy Roy DeKodes the Data | DeKoder

claims.quote: In the 25 constituencies with the highest SIR deletion rates, the TMC had a swing against it of nearly 10.5% ... in the 25 constituency with the lowest SIR deletions, the swing against the TMC was down to only 5.3% ... [SIR] deletions almost doubled the swing against the TMC.
claims.kind: A reading of the effect on results
claims.rests: He does not name the data behind the two swing figures. The comparison sets the 25 seats that lost the most names against the 25 that lost the fewest, with nothing to allow for other ways those seats differ, and the episode does not define the rate it calls the deletion rate.
claims.site: West Bengal's own figures show why other differences matter. Measured by the fall in the roll, the most affected districts are Kolkata North at 27.98 per 100 and Kolkata South at 24.54, and the least affected is Purbo Medinipur at 1.64. By seat the range runs from 39.74 in Chowrangee to 0.34 in Patashpur, so the seats at either end sit in different parts of the state with different histories of voting. In Bihar, the one state with a fitted model of the swing in these figures, leaving out each seat's lead at the previous election turns a slope of +0.31 into -0.83.
claims.stops: No swing model has been fitted for West Bengal. A vote count also cannot show whether the names left off or deleted moved votes from one party to another.

claims.quote: women deletions accounted for 62% of all deleted names compared with only 38% of men voters deleted.
claims.rests: The figure matches the Sabar Institute's count as BehanBox reported it, 61.8 per cent. That count takes names left off or deleted and names held for adjudication together.
claims.site: The Chief Electoral Officer's own counts give smaller shares. Women were 53.5 per cent of the 58.2 lakh names left off the draft, against 49.2 per cent of the roll, and 52.6 per cent of the fall from the 2024 roll to the roll at the 2026 nominations. They were over-represented in 21 of 24 districts.
claims.stops: The Chief Electoral Officer has published no split by sex of the adjudication outcomes, so the larger figure cannot be checked.

claims.quote: In other words, the SIR deletion process clearly targeted Muslim voters ... Muslim voter deletions were at a 52% higher deletion rate than non-Muslims.
claims.rests: He does not say how the religion of the electors left off or deleted was found. It can only be guessed from names, as the Sabar Institute did. His rate comparison is consistent with his own figures, 30 lakh against 19.8 lakh. The word targeted is a claim about purpose drawn from a pattern.
claims.site: The names West Bengal left off or deleted are not classified here by religion. In Bihar, where it does, the religion of those left off is guessed from names and given as a range, because some names cannot be classified. The census share falls inside that range in 18 of 38 districts and below it in 20.
claims.stops: Names give only a guess at religion, and the lists record no purpose. The figures make no claim about what anyone intended.

claims.quote: there's no doubt and there never has been any doubt that election [rolls] need to be constantly updated and cleaned up

strongest: The shares left off the draft that he gives for Delhi, Maharashtra and Karnataka, about 33, 21 and 20 per cent, are right as reported.
He asks the Commission to explain the gaps by sex and by religion, and no published data answers that.
further: Saying the names left off or deleted almost doubled the swing reads a cause into a raw comparison of two groups of seats.
Saying the process clearly targeted Muslim voters asserts a purpose that the figures cannot show.
He says the millions left off will now be unable to vote, which leaves out the names put back through Form 6 and appeals.

people.name: The Bharatiya Janata Party
people.role: India's governing party. Its account of the SIR figures here comes from two videos on its official YouTube channel, posted in October 2026.
people.intro: Only the videos' titles and descriptions could be read. What is said in them and shown on screen was not, so the quotations are from the descriptions, and no speaker is named in either.

pieces.title: SIR: 8 Questions, 8 Clear Answers | Election Facts | BJP
“13 Crore Voters Deleted?”| The Real SIR Numbers Explained | #SIR | #BJP

claims.quote:
9.5 Crore+ (71%) — Absent, shifted or other categories
2.7 Crore+ (20%) — Deceased entries
1 Crore+ (7.6%) — Multiple/duplicate entries
claims.rests: It rests on the Commission's counts of names left off the drafts, by the reason recorded beside each.
claims.site: Across 31 states, 13,39,03,307 names were left off the drafts. Of these, 9,56,35,923 (71.4%) were entered as shifted, absent or other, 2,79,69,558 (20.9%) as dead and 1,01,48,459 (7.6%) as duplicates. The party's figures agree with these to the precision it gives.
claims.stops: A reason is what the officer wrote down, and nobody checked it. In Bihar, set against death records, the names entered as dead come to about 3.4 years of adult deaths at the right ages, but 52.0% of them are women against 43.4% of deaths.

claims.quote: Presenting the entire figure simply as “13 crore genuine voters deleted” does not reflect the category-wise breakup of the draft electoral rolls.
The Election Commission has also ordered a special drive to identify and enrol eligible voters who may have been left out during SIR.
claims.kind: A fact about how the revision was run
claims.rests: It rests on the Commission's letter of 1 October 2026 to every Chief Electoral Officer.
claims.site: The letter orders booth officers to compare the roll from before the revision with the current one, visit those missing from it at home and help those found eligible fill in Form 6.
claims.stops: No figures from the drive have been published.

claims.quote: The Election Commission’s published material states that SIR is intended to ensure that eligible voters are included while ineligible entries are removed, with mechanisms for claims, objections and appeals. In Bihar’s 2025 SIR, the final roll included about 7.42 crore electors, after additions and deletions during the revision process.
claims.rests: It rests on the Commission's stated purpose for the revision, and Bihar's final roll.
claims.site: Bihar's final roll of 30 September 2025 held 7,41,92,357 electors, which rounds to 7.42 crore. The Commission's total for June 2025 was 7,89,69,844, so the roll fell by 47,77,487 over the revision. 65,59,626 names were left off the draft and 3,66,742 deleted after it.
claims.stops: The sentence gives the end figure and leaves out the fall. The figures count names on the roll and cannot say who among those left off was eligible.

claims.quote: From the alleged removal of 13 crore voters to questions around Form 6, ECINET, Gen Z voters, the role of Election Commissioners, Vote Chori and AI — this video examines eight major questions surrounding the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) and the electoral-roll process.

strongest: Its split of the 13 crore by recorded reason is the Commission's own and agrees with the totals of the states' figures.
It is right that the 13 crore are names left off the drafts by recorded reason, and some were restored afterwards.
further: The split is offered as an answer to whether eligible electors were left off. The reasons are what officers wrote down, and the largest group, shifted, absent or other, cannot show whether those electors had moved.
The Bihar sentence gives the final roll of 7.42 crore and leaves out the fall from about 7.89 crore before the revision.

people.name: Gyanesh Kumar, and the Election Commission of India
people.role: Chief Election Commissioner of India since February 2025. The panel also carries statements the Commission issued in its own name.
people.intro: His words come from press conferences in August and October 2025 and his National Voters' Day statement of January 2026, as The Indian Express, The Wire and PTI reported them. The Commission's statements come from its clarification of 23 September 2026 and its press note 120 of 26 September, as The Hindu and NDTV reproduced them and as the Commission published the press note.

pieces.title: Give affidavit in 7 days or apologise to nation: CEC to Rahul as his Bihar yatra hits the road
On Bihar Election Trail, Shah Brings Up 'Illegal Immigrants' on Rolls, But EC Provided No Figures
SIR rollout in remaining States soon: CEC Gyanesh Kumar
Dissent row: Election Commission says highlighting certain internal notes gives only one side of the picture
Election Commission "Fact-Checks" Rahul Gandhi's Form 6 Allegations

claims.quote: Halafnama dena hoga ya desh se maafi maangni hogi, koi teesra vikalp nahi hai… Agar saath din mein halafnama nahi mila to iska arth, ki yeh saare aarop niradhar hai.
claims.translation: Either give an affidavit or apologise to the nation, there is no third option. If an affidavit is not received within seven days, it would mean that these allegations are baseless. (The Indian Express's translation.)
claims.rests: The Express gives his Hindi words in Roman script with its own translation. The test he sets is whether an accuser signs an affidavit within seven days. At the same conference he did not say how many electors on the draft had submitted documents or how many foreign nationals had been found.
claims.site: Bihar's draft left off 65,59,626 names for four reasons as officers entered them. Officers entered 22,32,586 as dead, 26,55,900 as shifted, 9,70,081 as absent and 7,01,059 as already enrolled.
claims.stops: A reason is what the officer wrote down, and nobody checked it. Whether an affidavit is filed says nothing about whether the roll is right, and no record shows whether any allegation about it is true.

claims.quote: The names deleted from the electoral rolls include those who have died, those who are not Indian citizens, those who are registered in multiple places and those who have shifted permanently. The responsibility to create the electoral roll is of the ERO [electoral registration officer]. So every ERO and every district magistrate has this data
claims.kind: A fact about how the revision was run
claims.rests: He spoke at a press conference in Patna on 5 October 2025, five days after Bihar's final roll. The words are The Wire's English, and the language he spoke in was not found.
claims.site: None of the reasons in Bihar's published records is citizenship. The phase 1 lists give four reasons, dead, shifted, absent and already enrolled, for 65,59,626 names. After the draft the Commission's return lists 3,66,742 deleted, 62,441 as expired, 2,12,999 as shifted, 81,334 as repeated and 9,968 with no reason stated. In May 2026 the Supreme Court directed the Commission to refer any cases it had deleted as non-citizens to the authority under the Citizenship Act. Such cases may exist, and no count of them has been published.
claims.stops: The figures say nothing about whether any person is a citizen. A recorded reason is what an officer wrote down, and nobody checked it.

claims.quote: Many times, if any individual who is not an Indian citizen and who has got some papers made, you would have noticed, that in the enumeration phase we will match whether in 2002, 2003 or 2004, either you or your senior relatives were on the electoral rolls or not. If there is a match, then the matter ends there. Those who do not match, they will be issued a notice, after this they will have to show their papers and say where they were in 2003. Doing this is very necessary
claims.translation: The Wire's English; the original was likely Hindi and was not seen.
claims.kind: A fact about how the revision was run
claims.rests: He spoke when the Commission announced the second phase on 27 October 2025. The words are The Wire's English. He describes the procedure the order sets out.
claims.site: The order of 27 October 2025 asked for no documents at enumeration and sent notices after the draft to electors who could not be linked to the last intensive revision. Across the 21 states that have published a total, 13,06,52,476 electors kept on the drafts were sent a notice, 21.1 for every 100.
claims.stops: A notice records that an elector could not be linked to the old roll or that the entry showed a discrepancy. It is no finding about citizenship, and the figures never treat it as one.

claims.quote: The most compelling testament to the success of the SIR in Bihar was that not a single appeal was filed against the final electoral roll, establishing its sanctity and credibility
claims.rests: PTI quotes his statement of National Voters' Day, 24 January 2026, and NDTV quotes him saying the same on 27 October 2025. The count of appeals is the Commission's own and has not been published. Amit Shah said on 29 October 2025 that three appeals had been made against the deletions. Neither count is published, and the two may count different things.
claims.site: From the Commission's return, 65,59,409 names were left off Bihar's draft, 21,53,343 were added after it and 3,66,742 deleted, and the final roll of 7,41,92,357 is 47,72,808 smaller than the roll before. Counted from the lists of names left off, the figure is 65,59,626. The Commission's total for June 2025 was 7,89,69,844, and the final roll is 47,77,487 below it. The Supreme Court in May 2026 opened judicial review to people it called erroneously deleted as absent, dead, shifted or duplicate. In West Bengal, where adjudication outcomes were reported, 22,21,118 appeals were filed by people excluded, as reported.
